issues.legal_issue: An order of an absolute ruler continues as law only if it is legislative in character, rather than an executive step in negotiations leading to a contract.
material_facts: A prospective industrial promoter requested concessions, including a tax exemption, to induce the establishment of industries.
The ruler’s order approved the request and directed officials to proceed with the concessions; it was not published.
A formal written agreement incorporating the concessions was subsequently made between the government and the promoter.
issues.conclusion: The ruler’s order was not a law granting the tax exemption; it signified acceptance of the request and directed officials to take further steps toward the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 372 of the Constitution, the distinction between legislative, judicial and executive acts applies to orders of absolute rulers, and only orders that are jurisprudentially legislative continue as laws. The Court applied the approach in Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, State of Gujarat v. Vara Fiddali Badruddin Mithibar, and Rajkumar Narsingh Pratap Singh Deo v. State of Orissa; it explained that the general observations in Ameer-un-Nissa Begum v. Mehboob Begum and Director of Endowments, Government of Hyderabad v. Akram Ali did not eliminate that distinction. It also referred to Madhaorao Phalke v. State of Madhya Bharat regarding publication of laws.

rule.if: ruler_order_law_continuity_dispute and order_was_part_of_concession_negotiations and formal_contract_followed_order and order_was_not_published

predicates.ruler_order_law_continuity_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an order made by a ruler continued as law after a constitutional transition.
predicates.order_was_part_of_concession_negotiation: The ruler made the order while considering a prospective promoter’s request for concessions to establish an undertaking.
predicates.formal_contract_followed_order: The government and the prospective promoter later entered a written agreement incorporating the proposed concessions.
predicates.order_was_not_published: The ruler’s order was not published as a law.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns the continued legal force of a ruler’s order, and the order was part of concession negotiations, was followed by a formal contract, and was unpublished, the rule treats it as executive acceptance rather than law.

issues.legal_issue: The devolution of a pre-existing contractual obligation to the Union does not give the obligation constitutional immunity from competent legislation.
material_facts: The former ruler undertook by agreement to provide a tax exemption to an industrial undertaking.
The obligation passed through the successor state and devolved on the Union under the constitutional arrangements.
Parliament later enacted legislation concerning income taxation in the territory, and no constitutional limitation preventing that legislation was established.
issues.conclusion: The devolution of the contractual obligation did not prevent Parliament from enacting a valid law affecting or superseding it.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 294 and 295 provide for devolution of rights, liabilities and obligations and substitute the Union or successor states for the former governments; they do not change the essential character of contractual rights or liabilities or fetter legislative competence. Legislation within the legislature’s competence and consistent with constitutional limitations may affect those obligations. The Court relied on Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills Ltd. v. Union of India and State of Rajasthan v. Shyam Lal.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_inherited_contractua: The proceeding concerns a contractual obligation made by a predecessor government that is asserted against a successor government.
predicates.obligation_devolved_to_successor_governm: The predecessor government’s obligation passed to a successor government through a constitutional or governmental transition.
predicates.competent_legislation_addresses_contract: A legislature with authority over the subject enacted a law that addresses the subject of the inherited obligation.
predicates.no_constitutional_bar_to_legislation: No constitutional prohibition preventing the relevant legislation was established.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a contractual obligation inherited by a successor government, legislation within the legislature’s authority addresses its subject, and no constitutional prohibition applies, that legislation can affect the inherited obligation.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-existing tax-exemption agreement does not entitle an undertaking to exemptions beyond the relief available under valid tax legislation and the applicable concessions mechanism.
material_facts: An industrial undertaking claimed a tax exemption under an agreement made with a former ruler.
The income-tax regime was extended to the successor territory, and legislation provided for taxation there.
A statutory power allowed the government to grant relief to avoid hardship, anomaly or difficulty, and an order under that power provided a process for industrial undertakings to seek concessions.
The undertaking received relief for one section of its business but was refused relief for another section.
issues.conclusion: The agreement’s exemption was superseded by the applicable legislative provisions; the undertaking was entitled only to generally available rate reductions and such relief as was granted under the concessions mechanism.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 13 of the Finance Act, 1950, section 60-A of the Income-tax Act, 1922, and clause 16 of the Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950. It held that the valid extension of the income-tax regime and the accompanying concessions provisions superseded the exemption claimed under the earlier agreement. Article 295(1)(b) did not make the agreement immune from that legislation.

predicates.proceeding_claims_tax_exemption_under_pr: The proceeding concerns a claim to tax exemption based on an agreement made with a predecessor government.
predicates.tax_law_validly_applies_to_successor_ter: A valid tax law applies to income arising in the territory after its governmental transition.
predicates.law_provides_discretionary_concessions_p: The applicable legal regime allows a government authority to consider and grant tax concessions to affected undertakings.
predicates.claimed_relief_exceeds_relief_granted_un: The undertaking claims exemption beyond the relief granted through the applicable concessions process.

issues.definition: If an undertaking claims an exemption under a predecessor government’s agreement, valid tax law applies, a concessions process is available, and the claimed relief exceeds what that process grants, the agreement provides no additional exemption.

issues.legal_issue: An intergovernmental agreement concerning the levy, collection or distribution of public revenues does not make a private tax-exemption contract binding under the constitutional provision authorizing such agreements.
material_facts: A company relied on an agreement between the Union and a successor state that accepted recommendations about continuing certain financial privileges and immunities.
The agreement was a composite agreement made under several constitutional provisions.

The company’s claimed exemption arose from a separate contract between a former ruler and a private enterprise, rather than an arrangement between the Union and a state about levy, collection or distribution of public revenues.
issues.conclusion: The agreement concerning the concessions to corporations was to be treated as made under Article 295(1)(b), not Article 278(1)(a); Article 278 did not make the private contract binding for its specified period.
issues.legal_principle: Article 278(1)(a), read with Article 278(2), concerns agreements between the Union and a Part B State about the levy, collection and distribution of public revenues, not private contracts granting tax exemptions. In context, levy and collection concern the assessment and collection of taxes, rather than legislative competence to impose them. The Court considered Articles 266, 268–272 and 277 and relied on Town Municipal Committee v. Ramchandra Vasudeo Chimote in construing the expression concerning taxes being lawfully levied. The relevant concessions provision in the intergovernmental agreement was treated as falling under Article 295(1)(b).

predicates.proceeding_relies_on_intergovernmental_t: The proceeding relies on an agreement between the national government and a successor state to support a claimed tax benefit.
predicates.private_contract_grants_tax_exemption: The claimed tax benefit originates in a contract between a predecessor government and a private enterprise.
predicates.intergovernmental_agreement_concerns_cor: The intergovernmental agreement addresses concessions to corporations rather than arrangements for administering or distributing public revenues.

issues.definition: When a claim relies on an intergovernmental tax agreement but the exemption comes from a private contract and the intergovernmental agreement concerns corporate concessions rather than revenue administration, that agreement does not bind the national government to the private exemption.
